title: Google Workers Petition Sundar Pichai for Layoff Protections Amid AI Push
excerpt: More than 4,500 Google employees have signed a petition demanding guaranteed severance, voluntary buyouts, and an end to forced performance rankings as the tech giant accelerates AI investment.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 4,500 Google employees signed a petition for stronger layoff protections amid AI investments.
  • Demands include guaranteed severance, voluntary buyouts, and an end to performance rating quotas.
  • The petition is the largest job security effort at Google, growing from 1,250 signatures in early 2025.
  • Concerns are heightened for immigrant workers on employment-tied visas amid ongoing layoffs in tech.
  • Over 4,500 Google employees signed a petition delivered to CEO Sundar Pichai's office demanding stronger layoff protections.
  • Key demands include guaranteed severance, voluntary buyouts before mandatory layoffs, severance as extended paid leave, and an end to forced performance rating quotas.
  • The campaign, led by the Alphabet Workers Union-CWA, is the largest employee-organized job security effort at Google, growing from 1,250 signatures in early 2025 to 4,500 today.
  • The petition comes as tech companies across Silicon Valley reshape their workforces around AI, raising particular concerns for immigrant workers on employment-tied visas.

Members of the Alphabet Workers Union delivered a petition signed by more than 4,500 Google employees to CEO Sundar Pichai's office at the company's California headquarters on Thursday, demanding stronger protections against layoffs as Alphabet pours billions into artificial intelligence.

A staff member at Pichai's office accepted the petition and said it would be passed on to the CEO, according to The Guardian, which first reported the delivery. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Four Core Demands

The petition, organized under the banner "Googlers for Job Security," lays out four demands: guaranteed severance packages matching those offered during Google's 12,000-person layoff in January 2023, voluntary buyout options before any mandatory layoffs across all product areas, the option to receive severance as extended paid leave rather than a lump sum, and the elimination of what employees describe as quota-driven performance ratings under Google's GRAD (Googler Reviews and Development) system.

"The company is clearly in a strong financial position, making the loss of so many valuable colleagues without explanation hurt even more."

- Alphabet Workers Union petition

Parul Koul, a software engineer and president of the Alphabet Workers Union-CWA Local 9009, pointed to Alphabet's $4 trillion market valuation — which she said has quadrupled over the past six years — while criticizing ongoing workforce reductions. The union describes the petition as the largest employee feedback initiative at Google focused on job security.

A Campaign That Grew Steadily

The Googlers for Job Security campaign launched in late 2024 following multiple rounds of mass layoffs. When it debuted on internal channels in January 2025, it had roughly 400 signatures. By early 2025, CNBC reported the count had crossed 1,250. The petition grew to more than 3,800 signatures by April 2026, when union members staged simultaneous petition drives across Google campuses during Alphabet's Q1 earnings call.

The campaign has already produced results. Voluntary exit packages have been offered to more than 70,000 Google employees since the effort began, with the most recent round in February 2026 covering workers in Global Business & Operations and Platforms & Devices. Pichai himself acknowledged the program was implemented after listening to employees, saying "it gives people agency."

No other major tech company has adopted a comparable voluntary exit program, according to the union.

AI Investment and Workforce Anxiety

The petition arrives as Alphabet accelerates its AI spending. During the company's latest earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi described AI as a key investment priority, saying the company plans to continue hiring while increasing spending to support its AI ambitions. Google Cloud laid off some employees around two months ago, and the company eliminated more than a third of managers overseeing smaller teams last year, according to CNBC.

Google has not drawn a direct line between AI investment and layoffs. Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, told Wired that companies attempting to replace software developers with AI demonstrate "a lack of imagination." But the broader pattern across Silicon Valley tells a different story: Microsoft recently cut roughly 4,800 jobs as it increased AI spending, Oracle disclosed that wider AI adoption could continue reducing its workforce after cutting about 21,000 jobs over the past year, and Block reduced its headcount by some 4,000 employees with CEO Jack Dorsey citing AI-driven efficiency gains.

The Visa Dimension

For thousands of Indian-origin tech workers in the United States, the layoff anxiety carries an additional burden. Workers on H-1B visas typically have 60 days to find new employment after losing a job before they must leave the country. The Alphabet Workers Union has specifically highlighted this vulnerability, with one of its demands — severance as extended paid leave — designed to keep workers on the company payroll longer, effectively extending the window for visa holders to secure new positions.

In previous organizing rounds, the union called for a 180-day transfer window for affected workers, citing barriers faced by employees on employment-tied visas. Indians account for roughly 73% of all H-1B visa holders in the United States, making this a disproportionately Indian concern within Google's workforce.

What Comes Next

The union has requested that Pichai acknowledge receipt of the petition and respond to its demands within two weeks of delivery. Whether Google engages substantively remains to be seen. The company has historically maintained that employee evaluations are based on individual roles and expectations, and has denied imposing fixed rating distributions.

The petition is part of a broader reckoning in the technology industry, where a separate lawsuit filed against Meta by 26 anonymous employees alleges the company used AI-assisted tools to target workers on medical and parental leave for layoffs — claims Meta has denied. Together, these developments signal that the era of frictionless big tech layoffs may be giving way to organized employee pushback.

›H-1B visa holders have 60 days to find new jobs after layoffs.
›73% of H-1B visa holders in the U.S. are Indian-origin.
